blocks.md:
"Walk me through what happens to the three statements when…" is the single most common technical question at spring-week and summer-internship interviews. It is popular because it cannot be memorised as a fact: you have to *move* a number through the income statement, the cash flow statement and the balance sheet in the right order and prove it balances at the end.

The good news is that every version of the question — depreciation, inventory, a debt raise, a write-down — uses the same three links. Learn the links once and the walkthroughs become mechanical.

blocks.heading: Three statements, three links
blocks.md:
Each statement answers a different question about the same company over the same period:

- **Income statement (IS)** — *did we make a profit?* Revenue down to net income, on an accruals basis (recorded when earned, not when the cash moves).
- **Cash flow statement (CFS)** — *where did the cash actually go?* Starts from net income, fixes the non-cash items, then shows investing and financing.
- **Balance sheet (BS)** — *what do we own and owe right now?* A snapshot; assets = liabilities + equity, always.

The links that tie them together:

1. **Net income → CFS.** The first line of the cash flow statement is net income from the income statement.
2. **Net income → BS.** Net income (less dividends) flows into *retained earnings* inside shareholders' equity.
3. **Closing cash → BS.** The last line of the cash flow statement is the change in cash, which updates the cash line of the balance sheet.

Anything else on the balance sheet that changes (PP&E, inventory, debt) also appears somewhere on the CFS, which is how the whole thing stays balanced.

The order to walk in is always **IS → CFS → BS**, and the sanity check at the end is *assets − liabilities − equity = 0*.

**Income statement.** Work out the effect on operating profit, then apply tax. With a tax rate $t$, a pre-tax change of $\Delta$ changes net income by $\Delta \times (1 - t)$.

**Cash flow statement.** Start with the change in net income. Then *undo* anything that was in net income but was not cash (depreciation, amortisation, write-downs, stock-based pay) and *add* anything that was cash but not in net income (capex, working-capital movements, debt raised or repaid). The total is the change in cash.

**Balance sheet.** Update cash (from the CFS), update whichever other asset or liability moved, and update retained earnings by the change in net income. Then check both sides.

One rule of thumb that saves time: on the balance sheet, an **asset going down** (other than cash) is a **source of cash**; an **asset going up** is a **use of cash**. Liabilities are the reverse.

tmt.heading: Software: the cash arrives before the revenue
tmt.md:
A software company usually bills a year up front. The cash lands immediately, but accounting rules only let it recognise the revenue as the service is delivered — a month at a time. The unearned part sits on the balance sheet as **deferred revenue**, a liability: a promise to deliver, not money owed to a lender.

So the walk runs differently. Cash rises now; revenue and net income rise later. On the cash flow statement the increase in deferred revenue is a *working-capital inflow*, which is why fast-growing subscription businesses often show operating cash flow well above net income.

The second-order point interviewers want: deferred revenue growth is a **leading indicator**. If it stalls while revenue still climbs, the business has stopped signing new commitments and revenue will follow it down a few quarters later.
tmt.example_q: A SaaS company bills £12m for a year of service on 1 January. Walk me through the statements on that day, and then at the end of March.
tmt.answer_md:
On 1 January nothing has been delivered, so there is no revenue and no effect on the income statement. Cash rises £12m and deferred revenue — a liability — rises £12m. The balance sheet balances with no change to equity.

By 31 March three months have been delivered, so £3m moves out of deferred revenue into revenue. Net income rises by £3m less tax; deferred revenue falls to £9m; retained earnings rise by the after-tax profit. No cash moves in that second step — it already arrived in January.

healthcare.heading: Biotech: the spending is expensed, the value is not on the balance sheet
healthcare.md:
A biotech spends years on research before it sells anything. Under both IFRS and US GAAP, research is **expensed as incurred** — it hits the income statement immediately and almost never becomes an asset. So the walk starts from large, persistent losses that are entirely real cash going out of the door.

The consequence is the thing to say out loud: the balance sheet of a clinical-stage biotech tells you almost nothing about what the company is worth. Its main asset — a drug programme that might be worth billions — appears nowhere, because you are not allowed to capitalise it. What you see instead is cash, and the number every analyst watches is the **cash runway**: cash divided by quarterly burn.

That is also why these companies raise equity so often, and why a raise is a normal financing event rather than a distress signal.
healthcare.example_q: A biotech spends £40m on R&D this year and has no revenue. Walk me through the statements, and tell me what you would look at on the balance sheet.
healthcare.answer_md:
R&D of £40m is expensed, so operating profit and pre-tax profit both fall £40m. With no profits there is no tax to save, so net income falls the full £40m. On the cash flow statement you start at −£40m with nothing material to add back, so operating cash flow is roughly −£40m. On the balance sheet cash falls £40m and retained earnings fall £40m — it balances, and no asset is created.

On the balance sheet I would look at cash against the quarterly burn to get the runway. If that is under about eighteen months, a raise is coming, and that matters more to the equity story than any single line on the income statement.

blocks.prompt: Depreciation rises by £10m and the tax rate is 25 %. What happens to the company's cash?

options.label: Cash is unchanged — depreciation is non-cash

blocks.explain_md: Depreciation never moves cash directly — but it *is* deductible, so it cuts the tax bill. Operating profit falls £10m, tax falls by £10m × 25 % = £2.5m, and that saved tax is real money the company keeps. Net income falls £7.5m, you add the £10m back on the cash flow statement, and cash ends up **£2.5m higher**. The tax shield is the whole point of the question.

blocks.md: **Depreciation goes up by £10m**, tax rate 25 %. This is the classic version — everyone gets asked it.

steps.label: CFS: net income + add back depreciation

blocks.md: Same company, but this time **depreciation rises by £20m** and the tax rate is **30 %**. Fill in the three numbers that matter — the rest are done for you.

**"Depreciation is a cost, so cash goes down."**

No — depreciation is an *accounting* charge that spreads the cost of a machine you already paid for. The cash left when you bought the machine (capex, years ago). Recording depreciation today lowers profit and therefore lowers **tax**, which is real cash. So higher depreciation actually leaves the company with slightly *more* cash: the £2.5m tax saving in the example.

The related trap is forgetting tax altogether and saying net income falls by the full £10m. Interviewers listen for the $(1 - t)$.

If depreciation rises by £10m at a 25 % tax rate: on the income statement operating profit falls by £10m, tax falls by £2.5m, so net income is down £7.5m. On the cash flow statement net income is down £7.5m but depreciation is non-cash so I add the £10m back, and cash is up £2.5m. On the balance sheet cash is up £2.5m and PP&E is down £10m, so total assets are down £7.5m; on the other side retained earnings are down £7.5m through net income. Both sides fall by £7.5m, so it balances.

blocks.prompt: A company buys **£20m of inventory on credit** (it has not paid the supplier yet). Walk through the three statements at the moment of purchase, then say what changes when the inventory is sold for £30m in cash a month later (ignore tax on the sale for the first pass, then add it at 25 %).
blocks.model_answer_md:
**At purchase.** Income statement: nothing — no sale has happened, and inventory is not an expense until it is sold. Cash flow statement: inventory up £20m is a use of cash (−20), but accounts payable up £20m is a source (+20), so net change in cash is zero. Balance sheet: inventory +20 (asset), accounts payable +20 (liability). Balances, no cash moved.

**At sale (before tax).** Income statement: revenue +30, cost of goods sold +20, operating profit +10. Cash flow statement: net income +10, inventory falling by 20 is a source of cash (+20), so cash is up 30 — exactly the sale proceeds. Balance sheet: cash +30, inventory −20 → assets +10; retained earnings +10. Balances.

**With 25 % tax.** Net income is +7.5 instead of +10; cash is up 27.5 (30 received less 2.5 tax, assuming tax is paid in cash); assets +7.5, retained earnings +7.5. Still balances.
rubric: Says the income statement is untouched at the moment of purchase
Shows the inventory and payables movements cancelling on the cash flow statement
At sale, records revenue and cost of goods sold separately
Applies tax with (1 − t) and re-checks the balance

pairs.q: Which line appears on all three statements?
pairs.a: Net income: it closes the income statement, opens the cash flow statement and flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet.

pairs.q: If you could only see one statement, which would you pick?
pairs.a: The cash flow statement — it shows what actually happened to cash and lets you reconstruct much of the other two.

pairs.q: Accounts receivable rises by £5m. Cash effect?
pairs.a: Cash down £5m: customers owe more, so revenue was booked that has not been collected.

pairs.q: Why does a £10m write-down of an asset not reduce cash by £10m?
pairs.a: It is a non-cash charge — like depreciation, it lowers profit and tax but the cash left long ago (if ever). Cash actually rises by the tax saving.

blocks.md: **Net income links the income statement to both the others; the change in cash closes the loop — walk IS → CFS → BS and check it balances.**
